prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and for showing how reallocation of resources across firms shapes the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part on B005 with Melitz and Helpman. The reason is the directness of the evidence. Melitz (2003) shows that exposure to trade triggers selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms. This produces an aggregate productivity gain that industry-level models could not generate. Firm and transaction data from many countries have tested the prediction for more than twenty years. The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple analysis of exporting versus foreign direct investment extends the same selection logic to the organisation of multinational activity, and Helpman's wider work on trade and firm organisation supports a joint credit. The idea also reaches beyond trade. It is part of the micro-to-macro link between firm dynamics, reallocation and aggregate productivity that runs through modern growth and productivity research. The round 1 exchange did not move me off B005, but it did narrow the gap. Hassler's argument for the clean attribution and maturity of B011 is strong. I now regard B011 and B005 as close, and I would not oppose a two-name B011 with a narrow citation. I would not move B001 up, because it is more recent and the weight of credit supply versus other housing-boom explanations is still contested. Proposed wording for the public record: "for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and for showing how reallocation of resources across firms shapes the gains from trade." The wording says nothing about the discovery of exporter-premium facts, the Ricardian quantitative strand, or the monopolistic-competition base recognised in 2008. These assessments rest on general knowledge and I have not independently verified any source.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related empirical and theoretical contributions, and none is credited on this entry. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter facts the theory had to explain. Eaton and Kortum built a different, Ricardian strand with a different structure. Even narrow wording cannot fully remove the risk that a Helpman-Melitz citation overstates the priority of that pair. The second reservation is overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize. Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work sits in the lineage Krugman was recognised for, so his marginal credit rests on the heterogeneous-firm and firm-organisation work. Some welfare conclusions depend on functional forms such as Pareto productivity and CES demand. A committee that treats B011's single-paper origin as decisive for attribution, or that finds the 2022 overlap lighter than B005's 2008 overlap, could reasonably put B011 first. I cannot rule that out from the scientific record, and I do not treat the number of members preferring either entry as evidence of merit.

responses.point: Hassler holds that B011 is the clean two-person origin of the collateral-price feedback, that it is mature and tested, and that the 2022 prize covers distinct ground. He also says Helpman's earlier work overlaps with the 2008 trade prize and that attribution around Melitz is contested.
responses.response: I accept the attribution contrast. The B011 credit line is simpler than the B005 line, and the 2022 overlap is lighter than I assumed in my opening ranking, where I placed it seventh. Where I still differ is on evidence. The selection and reallocation margins have been observed directly in firm-level data across many countries, while the size of the collateral channel is established more through its repeated use as a modelling building block. I therefore answer the chair's question as follows. Yes, I would support a two-name B011 if the citation names only the collateral-price feedback and states that the accelerator strand is not being honoured. I would not make the attribution gap on B005 decisive, because I think wording can manage it. The two cases seem close to me, and I take your attribution point as a real mark in B011's favour.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B011 first but names B005 as his first alternative. He sees Melitz as a strong central contribution and Helpman's role as well supported. He says the difference is that Krugman's 2008 prize and the uncredited Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum make priority contestable, and he would go to B005 if the 2022 overlap proves decisive.
responses.response: That framing is fair and close to mine in reverse. The chair asked me to state Helpman's marginal credit separately from Krugman 2008 and from B020. My reading is as follows. Krugman's recognition concerned trade driven by scale economies and love of variety, and the location of production. Helpman's credit here concerns firm-level selection, the export-versus-FDI decision under heterogeneity, and the organisation of firms across borders. The Helpman-Melitz-Rubinstein work on zero trade flows is also part of making the firm margin empirically operational. None of this relies on the protection-for-sale work in B020, which I would leave out. The approach is credible but not free of risk. If the committee judged that a Melitz-only credit was safer, I would not oppose it, but I think the pair better reflects the theory-plus-extension structure of the achievement. I also agree with your view that if the 2022 overlap is judged decisive against B011, the committee should go to B005. Your point that the choice between the two is close is one I share.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B005 second and holds it as her first alternative. She names two reservations: the contested priority because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited, and the fact that Krugman's 2008 prize covers the new trade theory on which this work builds.
responses.response: Those are the two objections I weigh most, and I agree that neither disappears with wording. On priority, I draw the line between theory and empirical discovery. The Bernard-Jensen facts motivated the model and are not the achievement being cited. Melitz's contribution is a tractable model that unifies exporter selection, within-industry reallocation and gains from trade, which is what the proposed wording describes. On Krugman, I would put the burden on the citation to show that the contribution is selection and reallocation, not scale economies or variety gains. Your handling of B011 (Hassler's argument moved you to a narrow two-name proposal) is a model for how I would handle B005: a narrow citation, no extra names, and an explicit statement of what is not covered. I do not consider your ranking of B011 above B005 unreasonable.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from B019 to B005 in round 1. The point is that the way to handle the uncredited contributors is to word the citation around the heterogeneous-firm selection model and its welfare implications, without claiming the whole empirical firm-trade literature. Fredriksson also qualifies the claim that the 2007-09 crisis confirmed the collateral mechanism, since the channel is hard to identify directly.
responses.response: I agree on the wording strategy, and it is the basis of the citation I propose. I also agree on the identification point about B011, which is why I count the firm-level testing of B005 as a real advantage. I would add one caution to your argument. Direct testing of the selection margin does not settle every welfare number. The gains from trade depend on functional-form assumptions, so the citation should speak about the mechanism and not about a measured size of gains. Applying the same standard to B011, the committee should credit the mechanism and not a measured amplification magnitude. Holding both candidates to that standard makes the comparison fairer, and I think it leaves the two close.

uncertainties: Whether wording alone can handle the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, or whether the committee will see a Helpman-Melitz pairing as overstating the priority of that pair.

How much marginal credit Helpman has beyond the lineage covered by Krugman's 2008 prize, and whether a Melitz-only credit would be more defensible on attribution grounds even if it undersells the extensions.

Whether the 2022 overlap for B011 is as light as Hassler, Krusell and Stromberg argue. If it is, B011's cleaner attribution may outweigh B005's more direct empirical record, and the committee could reasonably choose B011.

I could not find a coherent two-part configuration under the three-person cap: B005 with two names plus a two-name B011 would need four people. A single part is therefore my working assumption, and that choice is a judgement about the strength of the individual cases.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied committee text. I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile shows frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell (secretary) and co-authorship with John Hassler (chair), and both are IIES colleagues. Both prefer B011, and I address their arguments above on the merits and not as a result of those ties. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, who is credited in B016. B016 is not in my preferred configuration, and I ranked it sixth in my opening. I also collaborate with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li on creative destruction and growth measurement. That work is thematically close to the firm-reallocation theme in B005 and could make me favour B005, so I have tried to hold it to the same evidence standard as B011. The profile shows no direct connection to Helpman, Melitz or Redding, and none to Kiyotaki, Moore, Mian or Sufi. The profile suggests I may have helped draft the 2025 Scientific Background, but that is weak evidence and has no bearing on this ballot. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
